title: Ernest McLean and the guitar as soloist
summary: He praises young Ernest McLean's single-note technique, though not as a rhythm man, and would feature him as soloist.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: I have, have you ever heard young Linus McLean play the guitar? Yes, not very much.
Well he's another Les Paul, believe me. I've heard him really, really stick out.
Heard his father a lot more on bass, but you say his father was a guitar player.
Yes, he's a guitar player, along in my class. But Linus, I mean, put both of us in the sewer.
Linus is great. As far as that type of thing.

He's a guitar player, he has, and a single note technician. And I've heard he's not very much as a chord man in a band. But man, he has technique on the single note man. And he makes chords so far as the number he's playing it goes. But I mean for a rhythm man in a band, he's not much a rhythm man. Because he knows chords. He can take any part in an orchestration. And he'd play it on the guitar, trombone, clarinet, anybody's part. He'd play it on the guitar.
What do you think is the main job of the guitar in a band?

Now okay, a guitar is entitled to a soloist, well as nobody else in a band. If he's a soloist, and Ernest is one, I'll tell you what, if I was able to have a band, I would like to have Ernest as a first guitarist. All I want to do is play rhythm. But I want to feature him on solo. Circus solo. For St. Joe.
